sections.text: WS-POL-D – Definitions Analysis

The clearest overall conclusion is that WS-POL-D was never just a glossary exercise. Definitions became one of the committee’s most important policy levers because terms like AI assistance, AI literacy, AI detector, approved tool, high-stakes use, disclosure, and human decision-maker determine how later sections on integrity, student use, staff use, privacy, and accountability actually work in practice.

heading_path: Core conclusion
sections.text: The strongest evidence in the public record points to four main definition disputes. First, whether the definitions section should be mostly neutral and descriptive or should carry normative policy content. Second, whether AI literacy should be defined mainly as practical fluency with AI tools or equally as knowing when not to use AI. Third, whether citation and disclosure should be treated as closely related or as distinct ethical obligations. Fourth, how AI assistance should be defined for purposes of disclosure, restrictions, and integrity review—especially whether the trigger should be a “material contribution” test, a functional/tiered test, or an inclusive definition with explicit exemptions. These are not side issues; they shape the whole policy shell.

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: Meeting 3 is the clearest starting point. Thomas Colvin said the baseline document already contained “current definitions” of AI, AI language models, large language models, and generative AI, and explained that the purpose of those definitions was to demystify AI by showing that these systems are ultimately statistical tools, “basically just math,” and not magical systems that always give the right answer. In the same exchange, he said Elizabeth Chua had “schooled” him on the breadth of AI literacy, and that her additions were intended to help the committee get on the same page about what the term means. So from the start, the definitions work was doing two things at once: technical demystification and normative framing. (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: John Black’s process framing in the same meeting helps explain why definitions became so important. He emphasized that the committee had to identify principles and tradeoffs, that values collide, and that the group needed enough clarity to reduce uncertainty and produce useful, flexible policy. Thomas Colvin also pressed for clarity about what a “principle” even is. In that setting, definitions were not merely about clarity of wording. They became a way to decide which assumptions were acceptable, which distinctions mattered, and where the committee wanted to place hidden policy judgments. (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: By the time the V3 outline was posted, definitions had become a standalone section with an explicit list of key terms: AI, Generative AI, AI detector, Approved tool, High-stakes use, AI assistance, Disclosure / attribution, Human decision-maker, Vendor / data processor / routine use / consent terms as needed. That list is revealing because it mixes ordinary definitional terms with terms that are already deeply bound up with later decisions in staff use, student use, privacy, and accountability. In other words, the outline itself shows that the committee had come to treat the definitions section as a policy architecture section, not just a vocabulary appendix.

heading_path: What the workstream products say
sections.text: The early policy shell in D-POL-1 confirms that definitions were meant to sit very near the top of the policy logic. In the decision log, “Definitions” appears immediately after “Scope & Triaging,” before the sections on staff use, student use, privacy, and public accountability. That placement implies the committee understood definitions as a prerequisite for applying restrictions, disclosure expectations, and governance rules consistently. (GitHub)

heading_path: What the workstream products say
sections.text: The strongest evidence that definitions were already carrying policy choices comes from David Berol’s WS-POL-D draft. His contribution does not just define “generative AI” technically. It also defines AI literacy as including both technical and pragmatic instruction, but then argues that the “core” of AI literacy is understanding where AI use is and is not appropriate. He goes further by defining constructive feedback, evaluative feedback, assessment, AI detector, citation, and disclosure in ways that explicitly support his later positions on teacher feedback, academic integrity, and student process evidence. This is important because it shows one committee strategy very clearly: use definitions to settle later policy fights in advance.

heading_path: What the workstream products say
sections.text: The Meeting 4 packet shows that the committee recognized this problem directly. In the Red Zone, D2 — Definition Lock: AI Assistance is treated as a formal decision, with three rewrite families under consideration: a material contribution definition, a tiered functional definition, and an inclusive plus exempt-list approach. The packet also says this definition affects disclosure, restriction rules, classroom examples, tool approval, and integrity review. That is perhaps the single clearest piece of evidence that the committee understood definitions—especially “AI assistance”—as the hinge connecting multiple workstreams.

heading_path: What the workstream products say
sections.text: Jillian Burkley’s D-DPS draft shows a third approach to definitions: operational governance definitions. Her work effectively defines “approved tool,” “high-risk” use, “identity-linked” systems, “consequential use,” “student artifacts,” “data processing agreement,” and related governance concepts by tying them to a three-tier review structure and approval requirements. That means the privacy/governance workstream was not waiting for WS-POL-D to resolve everything. It was already operationalizing some definitions in a way that would strongly influence what “approved tool,” “high-stakes,” “vendor,” or “data processor” would have to mean in the policy.

heading_path: What the workstream products say
sections.text: The equity workstream reinforces that definitions must work across multiple domains. D-EQA-1 says its review should apply to policy language, guidance, tools, and workflows and asks reviewers to specify target users, settings, grade bands, and data touched. Its integrity/fairness prompts ask what evidence besides detectors will be used and what evidence is explicitly prohibited. This suggests that several definition terms—especially AI assistance, detector, approved tool, and high-stakes use—must be written in ways that work not just for classroom policy, but also for equity review and implementation practice. (GitHub)

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: The committee seems to have broad agreement on at least three definition priorities. First, definitions should be plain-language and usable, not merely technically correct. Thomas Colvin’s Meeting 3 presentation framed definitions as a demystifying tool for the committee itself, and the values/process materials repeatedly emphasize clarity and applicability. Second, definitions must support grade-banded and context-specific application, because later sections depend on differences by age, subject, risk, and instructional purpose. Third, definitions should be good enough to reduce confusion across workstreams, especially around student use, staff use, integrity, and privacy. (GitHub)

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: The survey also suggests strong agreement that certain terms need clearer definition even when people differ on their eventual content. One survey response explicitly called for clarifying what qualifies as “AI use” so that grammar suggestions and generative drafting are not treated the same, and for defining “high-stakes” consistently across grade bands. Another supported grade-banded disclosure precisely because expectations need to be developmentally appropriate and proportionate to stakes. This suggests the committee largely agrees which terms need definition, even if it does not yet agree on the best wording. (GitHub)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Neutral/technical definitions vs. value-laden definitions
sections.text: One fault line is whether the definitions section should be mostly descriptive or should embed policy judgment. The Meeting 3 / RSB line leans toward technical demystification: define AI and related tools in plain terms, emphasize that they are statistical systems, and avoid magical framing. That approach keeps definitions relatively neutral and leaves most normative judgment to later sections. (GitHub)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Neutral/technical definitions vs. value-laden definitions
sections.text: David Berol’s draft represents the opposite tendency. His definitions are not only descriptive; they are interpretive. “AI literacy” becomes partly a philosophy of restraint. “Citation” and “Disclosure” are separated into two different ethical obligations. “Constructive feedback” and “Evaluative feedback” are defined in ways that strongly support later restrictions on teacher AI use. This is a coherent drafting strategy, but it is not neutral. It uses the definitions section to preload later policy conclusions.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
2. What counts as “AI assistance”?
sections.text: This is probably the most important live dispute. The Meeting 4 packet elevates it into a formal lock decision because it controls disclosure and restriction rules. A material contribution definition would likely focus on whether AI meaningfully shaped ideas, structure, or output. A tiered functional definition would vary with what the system actually did—grammar support, summarization, outlining, drafting, reasoning, etc. An inclusive plus exempt-list approach would define AI assistance broadly but then carve out minor aids such as spelling or grammar correction. Each approach reflects a different philosophy of enforcement and clarity.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
2. What counts as “AI assistance”?
sections.text: The survey suggests this was still unresolved. Some responses wanted simpler, clearer, more teachable disclosure rules. Others explicitly warned that simple binary rules around “AI use” or “high-stakes” were too blunt and that disclosure depends on exactly what the student used AI for, the grade band, the subject, and the presence of an assessment backstop. This tension mirrors the Meeting 4 options closely: precision and flexibility pull in different directions. (GitHub)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. What does “AI literacy” mean?
sections.text: The Meeting 3 transcript and the survey show that AI literacy itself was contested. Thomas Colvin presented it as something broad enough that Elizabeth had to expand it. David Berol then argued that AI literacy is often misheard as “use as much AI as possible so students are ready for the future,” and insisted instead that AI literacy includes knowing when not to use AI. Some survey comments approved that framing directly, while others thought the term was too vague or jargon-heavy unless rewritten more concretely. So even when members liked the phrase, they did not necessarily mean the same thing by it. (GitHub) (GitHub)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: David’s definitions draft makes the strongest internal distinction here. He argues that citation is an obligation owed to sources and intellectual lineage, while disclosure is an obligation owed to teachers and peers so evaluators can understand what labor was off-loaded to AI and assess student work fairly. That distinction is powerful and likely useful, but it is also more philosophically elaborated than the V3 outline, which simply lists “Disclosure / attribution” as a term. The public record does not show a clean committee-wide rejection of David’s distinction, but it also does not show that everyone embraced such a sharp conceptual split.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: The IB materials help explain why this distinction is live. The IB’s academic integrity policy says the goal of academic integrity is to make knowledge, understanding, and thinking transparent, and it requires that when students use AI-generated text or images, they must clearly reference the AI tool, include the prompt and date, and treat the material as something that must be made visible rather than hidden. That supports the idea that “disclosure” and “citation” are related but not identical functions. (International Baccalaureate®)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Approved tool, high-stakes use, human decision-maker, vendor/data processor
sections.text: These terms seem less debated philosophically and more underdeveloped across workstreams. The V3 outline clearly expects them to be defined. But the actual content is emerging from governance rather than from the definitions debate alone. D-DPS effectively provides the strongest available working definitions of “approved tool,” “consequential use,” identity linkage, and some vendor/data terms through its tiering and approval rules. That suggests one likely committee path forward: let WS-POL-D define these terms in brief, but harmonize them tightly with the D-DPS governance framework so they do not drift.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Approved tool, high-stakes use, human decision-maker, vendor/data processor
sections.text: External sources that illuminate the definition debate

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Approved tool, high-stakes use, human decision-maker, vendor/data processor
sections.text: Two external sources are especially useful because they match the committee’s own references. First, Arlington Public Schools’ guidance defines generative AI in plain language and treats its guidance as a living framework that supports responsible use, transparency, equity, and accountability. That supports a definitions section written in accessible, district-friendly language rather than in vendor or research jargon. (Arlington Public Schools)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Approved tool, high-stakes use, human decision-maker, vendor/data processor
sections.text: Second, the IB academic integrity policy is highly relevant because it links AI definitions directly to ethical practice. The IB explicitly says it will not ban AI, says students must be taught to use it ethically, and requires that if students use AI-generated text or images, they must clearly reference the AI tool, prompt, and date. That is a strong external analogue for FCCPS’s own emerging distinction between AI assistance, disclosure, and transparency. (International Baccalaureate®)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Approved tool, high-stakes use, human decision-maker, vendor/data processor
sections.text: A third useful analogue is the U.S. Copyright Office’s January 2025 AI report, which says AI-assisted works can still receive copyright protection where a human determines sufficient expressive elements, but that prompts alone are not enough to establish authorship. That is not a school policy source, but it is conceptually helpful for Definitions because it supports the idea that “AI assistance” is not the same thing as “AI authorship,” which in turn supports clearer thinking about disclosure, attribution, and authentic human work. (U.S. Copyright Office)

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: For drafting purposes, the safest committee-grounded common ground is this: definitions should be plain-language, operationally useful, developmentally and contextually applicable, and tightly aligned with later policy sections. The committee clearly needs clean definitions for at least Generative AI, AI detector, AI assistance, approved tool, high-stakes use, disclosure/attribution, human decision-maker, and vendor/data processor. The public record strongly supports saying that “AI assistance” is the most load-bearing definition because it affects disclosure, restrictions, integrity review, and classroom examples simultaneously.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Where you will have to choose your own stance is on how normative you want the definitions section to be. The accessible record supports at least three possible approaches. A minimal/neutral approach would define terms technically and leave most ethical or policy claims to later sections. A normative approach, closer to David’s, would intentionally shape later debates through the definitions themselves. A hybrid approach—which may be the most practical—would define the technical and governance terms neutrally, keep brief but useful distinctions like citation versus disclosure, and reserve the stronger value judgments for the substantive sections where dissent can be shown more transparently.
